Ibn Ḥanbal also answers a Jahmite argument based on the verse:
“The Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, is only the Messenger of God and His Word.” (Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, verse 171)
The Jahmites argued that Jesus was created, and if Jesus is called God’s Word, then God’s Word must also be created.
Ibn Ḥanbal replies that the Qurʾān uses many descriptions of Jesus that are never used of the Qurʾān itself.
Jesus is described as born, as a child, as a boy and as a grown man.
Can those same descriptions be applied to the Qurʾān?
“It is not lawful for us to say of the Qurʾān what we say of Jesus.”
When the Qurʾān calls Jesus “His Word,” Ibn Ḥanbal says, it refers to the creative command:
God said “Be” to Jesus, and Jesus came into existence.
He is not himself the word “Be.”
That word is speech, and the speech itself is not created.

Ibn Ḥanbal then continues by responding both to Christians and to Jahmites over expressions such as “the Word of God” and “the Spirit of God.” The discussion appears on page 30 of the work just mentioned.
We have presented these examples from Ibn Ḥanbal’s arguments so that his method becomes clear.
He limits himself to arguing from the religious texts.
He does not engage with the rational proofs used by the Muʿtazilites.
That is both his position and his method.
Some later Hanbalis went further than Ibn Ḥanbal himself.
They extended the eternity of the Qurʾān beyond its content and argued that the Qurʾān was eternal even in its letters and sounds.
Some went so far as to say:
“Even the leather and the cover are eternal, not only the Qurʾānic codex itself.”
“It is agreed that what lies between the two covers is the speech of God, and that what we read, hear and write is the speech of God.
“The words and letters themselves must therefore be the speech of God.
“And since it is agreed that God’s speech is uncreated, these words and letters must themselves be eternal and uncreated.”
“…until the age reached ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Kullābī, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qalānisī and al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī.

“These men belonged to the Salaf, but they took up the discipline of kalām. They defended the beliefs of the Salaf with theological arguments and systematic proofs. Some wrote books, while others taught.”
This statement marks the beginning of a new line within the picture we have just described.
With these thinkers, the Salafi current begins to take on a different form.

It moves beyond the absolute traditionalism of Mālik ibn Anas, beyond the simple refusal to interpret found among some Hanbalis, and beyond Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal’s limited interpretation based closely on the wording of scripture.
Yet it still remains within the wider Salafi framework.
Al-Shahrastānī is right to place these three thinkers—al-Kullābī, al-Qalānisī and al-Muḥāsibī—inside that framework.
All three belonged firmly to the People of the Sunna and the Community.
Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī said of the followers of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kullāb al-Qaṭṭān that:
“They hold most of what we have reported from the People of the Sunna.”
And, as we know, the People of the Sunna rejected the Muʿtazilite teachings on God’s attributes and on the created Qurʾān.
Ibn Kullāb himself, who died in 240 AH / 854 CE, affirmed eternal attributes of God, including speech.
He also accepted the traditional Sunni position on predestination: both good and evil come from God.

Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Khālid al-Qalānisī, who died around 255 AH / 868 CE, and al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī, who died in 243 AH / 857 CE, also appear to have belonged to Ibn Kullāb’s school.
Although this school remained Salafi in doctrine, it differed from earlier Salafism in the method it used.
It defended its beliefs and attacked the Muʿtazilites using the techniques of theological argument.
Al-Shahrastānī had already pointed this out.
Al-Subkī described ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kullāb as:
Al-Baghdādī said of al-Qalānisī that in his time he was a leading defender of Sunni belief:
“His writings on kalām exceeded one hundred and fifty books. Among them were a refutation of al-Naẓẓām, together with other books and treatises.”
Ibn Taymiyya also noted al-Muḥāsibī’s connection with the teachings of Ibn Kullāb.

From Ibn Taymiyya’s account of the Kullābite school, it appears that one of its innovations within Salafi doctrine was the claim that the Qurʾān was eternal and inseparable from God’s essence, and that God did not speak through an act of His will and power.
Earlier Salafis had usually gone no further than saying that the Qurʾān was uncreated and that God “has always been speaking,” or that “He speaks through His will and power.”
Ibn Taymiyya explains what the Kullābite school meant by saying that God does not speak through His will and power.
“The speaker is the one in whom speech exists, without that speech being produced by his own act, will or power.”
In other words, God’s speech is an attribute permanently belonging to His essence, not an act that He performs.
Because if God’s eternal speech were an act of divine will, then before human beings existed that speech would have been directed toward people who did not yet exist.
And if speech depended on divine will and power, it would mean that God had possessed the power to speak from eternity, including at a time when no one existed to hear Him.
Speech, they argued, requires both a speaker and someone being addressed.
If the second does not exist, speech itself does not occur.
Through this kind of theoretical reasoning, the Kullābite school took Salafi thought beyond its traditional reluctance to use reason in theology.
It began to follow the method of the theologians.
This was really an expression of a larger new intellectual development.

Rational theological thinking had apparently become so deeply rooted in religious thought that its influence now extended even to some of the most conservative thinkers, those who had previously been most resistant to the rational methods of kalām associated with the age of philosophy.
C — The Ashʿari current: It is very clear that Ashʿarism developed out of the Kullābite school.
After mentioning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿīd al-Kullābī, Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Qalānisī and al-Ḥārith ibn Asad al-Muḥāsibī and describing their use of kalām, al-Shahrastānī continues:

“…until Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī and his teacher entered into a debate over the question of what is good and what is best. They broke with one another, and al-Ashʿarī joined this group”—meaning the group of al-Kullābī, al-Qalānisī and al-Muḥāsibī.
“He then defended their position with the methods of kalām. This became the doctrine of the People of the Sunna and the Community, and the Ṣifātiyya developed into the Ashʿariyya.”
The appearance of al-Ashʿarī, who died in 330 AH / 941 CE, and of his theological school opposing the Muʿtazilites brought the traditionalist opposition into a more complete and systematic form.
From then on, the struggle against the Muʿtazilites increasingly used the same weapon the Muʿtazilites themselves had used: rational theological argument.
The two sides now formed parallel currents within the same wider intellectual movement—the theoretical inquiry that became the discipline of kalām.
But to say that Ashʿarism continued the Kullābite school means continuity mainly in method.
The details of their doctrines were not identical.
Al-Ashʿarī developed the theory of inner speech, an idea that Ibn Kullāb had already placed, more implicitly, at the foundation of his theory of God’s speech.
Ibn Kullāb argued that God’s speech is eternal.
For this reason, he said, it cannot literally be command, prohibition or report, because these are things that arise in time.
How can something eternal possess qualities that come into existence?
He therefore distinguished between two kinds of speech.
The first is eternal speech, one of God’s permanent eternal attributes.
The second is speech that arises when there are people to address, such as commands, prohibitions and reports.
The first belongs to God’s essence.
The second belongs to His acts.
Ibn Kullāb used a similar distinction when speaking of God as Creator.
The attribute of creation also has two forms: an eternal attribute inseparable from God’s essence, and the act of creation that occurs when something is actually created.
The first kind of divine speech—the eternal kind—is what al-Ashʿarī later called inner speech.
But al-Ashʿarī disagreed with Ibn Kullāb’s claim that eternal divine speech cannot contain commands, prohibitions and reports.
Al-Ashʿarī said that God’s speech has been command, prohibition and report from eternity.
The fact that the people being addressed did not yet exist creates no problem.
A person who does not yet exist can still be addressed on the assumption that he will exist.
The divine address is eternal and is directed toward the person who will later come into existence.
When that person finally exists, no new divine speech has to arise.
